description: Pre-production, production and post-production: how process and personnel shape the final product.
content_html:
From Idea to Audience: The Three Phases

Every media product — a television drama series, a magazine feature, a music video, a radio documentary — passes through three broad phases before it reaches an audience. Understanding these phases, the people involved and the technologies used is essential for explaining why media products look, sound and feel the way they do. The spec frames this as the relationship between pre-production, production and post-production.

Pre-Production: Planning the Work

Pre-production is everything that must be decided before a camera rolls or a microphone is switched on. It includes commissioning (deciding which projects to fund and develop), writing and developing the script, casting performers, scouting locations, drawing up a production schedule and agreeing a budget. The stronger the pre-production planning, the fewer expensive problems arise during filming or recording.

In television, a key pre-production role is the showrunner — the person who holds creative responsibility for an entire series. In film, the equivalent executive oversight often comes from a producer or executive producer. These roles shape the product before a single shot is taken, which is why pre-production decisions have such a strong influence on the finished work.

Key Fact

Pre-production includes commissioning, scripting, casting, scheduling and budgeting. These decisions shape the product’s genre, tone, form and intended audience before production even begins. Budget limits in pre-production often determine the visual style of the finished product.

Production: Making It

Production is the phase in which the actual filming, recording or other creative work takes place. A television drama may shoot on location, in a studio or a mixture of both. A radio documentary requires field recording and studio interviews. A magazine requires photography shoots, writing and design. Each media form has its own production conventions, but in all cases the production phase turns the pre-production plan into raw material.

Production teams vary enormously in size depending on the budget and form. A large-scale television production might employ hundreds of crew members; a podcast series might be produced by a single person with a laptop and a microphone. The size of the team, the technology available and the working environment all shape what kinds of product are possible.

Post-production is where raw footage or recordings are shaped into the finished product. For film and television, post-production includes editing, colour grading, adding visual effects, mixing the soundtrack and creating titles and credits. For music, it includes mixing and mastering. For print media, it includes layout, typesetting and image retouching.

Post-production has been transformed by digital technology. Work that once required large specialist facilities can now be completed on a standard laptop. This has lowered the barrier to entry for independent and lower-budget productions — and it means that post-production decisions (such as colour grading choices or editing rhythm) are now a significant part of the creative identity of a product, not merely technical finishing.

Outsourcing, the Freelance Economy and the Gig Economy

Major media organisations do not employ every person who works on their products. Much media production relies on outsourcing — contracting specialist companies or individual freelancers to provide specific services. A broadcaster might commission an independent production company to make a documentary series; a magazine might hire freelance photographers and writers for specific features.

This has created a large freelance economy in media. Many crew members, journalists, designers and technicians work on short-term contracts, moving from project to project. This gives organisations flexibility but can create instability for individual workers. Critics of the model, particularly in relation to digital media platforms, describe these conditions as part of a broader “gig economy” — one in which workers bear the financial risk of fluctuating demand rather than receiving the security of permanent employment.

Key Fact

Outsourcing reduces costs and increases flexibility for media organisations. However, it shifts financial risk onto individual freelance workers, creating a workforce that lacks permanent employment security — a pattern that has intensified in the digital era.

The rise of subscription streaming services has created a distinct working practice sometimes called streaming-first commissioning. Rather than making a film or series for theatrical release or broadcast window, a streaming platform commissions content directly for its own service — and may release all episodes of a series on the same day rather than one per week. This changes the economics of production (budgets and marketing are shaped around subscriber retention, not broadcast ratings) and can also change narrative structure (binge-viewing audiences tolerate different pacing than weekly viewers).

Understanding how the platform a product is made for shapes its working practices and form is a key analytical skill. A radio documentary, a social media vertical video and a prestige streaming drama series are all made through the three-phase process, but the personnel, technologies, schedules and budgets involved — and therefore the finished products — look very different.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to explain how production processes affect a media product, avoid simply listing the three phases as a sequence of events. The highest-mark answers connect a specific production decision — a budget constraint, an outsourcing choice, a streaming-first brief — to a specific observable quality in the finished product. Show that production conditions cause the content, rather than just describing both separately.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Every media product passes through pre-production (planning), production (creating) and post-production (editing and finishing) before it reaches an audience; decisions in each phase shape the final product.
  • Media industries rely heavily on outsourcing and freelance labour, giving organisations commercial flexibility while creating precarious working conditions for many workers.
  • Streaming-first commissioning has created new working practices in which budget, narrative structure and release strategy are all shaped by the demands of subscription platform economics.

practice_questions.text: Which phase of media production involves editing, colour grading and mixing the soundtrack?
practice_questions.marks: Post-production. Distractor check: pre-production = planning; production = filming/recording; commissioning = pre-production sub-phase.

practice_questions.text: Identify one role that is typically completed during the pre-production phase of a television drama.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any valid pre-production role: writing or developing the script, casting performers, scouting locations, drawing up a production schedule, agreeing a budget, commissioning.

practice_questions.text: Identify and explain how outsourcing affects the working practices of a large media organisation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying outsourcing (contracting external companies or freelancers to complete specific work). One mark for a clear explanation of its effect, e.g. it reduces the organisation's permanent workforce costs and allows flexibility, but means many workers are on short-term contracts rather than permanent employment.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'streaming-first commissioning' and how it differs from traditional broadcast working practices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise explanation of streaming-first commissioning; clear contrast with broadcast working practices in terms of release strategy, audience measurement and production economics; analytical engagement with how the commissioning platform shapes the product.
Secure: Accurate explanation of streaming-first; some contrast with broadcast drawn; limited analytical depth.
Developing: Basic explanation of what streaming-first means; contrast with broadcast vague or incomplete.
Emerging: Vague response; streaming and broadcast differences not clearly explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of freelance and outsourced labour shapes the working practices of the media industries, with reference to a specific media form.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise explanation of freelance and outsourced working practices; well-chosen, specific example from a named media form; clear link between working practice and its commercial or creative consequences for the organisation and/or the workers.
Secure: Clear explanation of outsourcing/freelance; relevant example; link to consequences made.
Developing: Some explanation; example present but underdeveloped or weakly linked.
Emerging: Basic or confused account; example missing or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how decisions made during pre-production and post-production shape the final form and meaning of a media product you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis connecting specific pre-production decisions (budget, casting, scripting) and post-production choices (editing rhythm, colour grade, sound design) to observable qualities in a named Close Study Product; argument about how production conditions determine meaning, not just content; relevant theoretical framing (e.g. industries framework).
Secure: Clear analysis of pre-production and post-production decisions; reference to a studied product; some connection between decisions and the finished product's qualities.
Developing: Some engagement with production phases; product referenced but analysis is mainly descriptive.
Emerging: Basic or confused account of production phases; mainly narrative or descriptive; reference to product minimal.

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes the person responsible for both the creative and day-to-day managerial oversight of an entire television series?
What is the main commercial advantage for a media organisation of using outsourced and freelance workers?
options: Reduced costs and increased workforce flexibility

knowledge_checks.q: The editing, colour grading and sound mixing applied to raw footage after the main shoot is known as _____.
Hiring external companies or individuals to carry out specific tasks rather than using in-house employees is called _____.
Match each production phase to its main activity.
right: Editing, colour grading and sound mixing
Filming, recording or creating the raw content

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of the pre-production phase?
flashcard_questions.a: To plan the entire production before filming or recording begins.
Editing, colour grading, sound mixing and finishing raw footage or recordings.
A senior figure holding creative and managerial responsibility for an entire TV series.

flashcard_questions.q: What is outsourcing in media production?
flashcard_questions.a: Hiring external companies or freelancers for specific tasks rather than using in-house staff.
Producing content primarily for a streaming platform, often releasing all episodes simultaneously.
A detailed timeline setting out when each stage of production happens and who is responsible.

flashcard_questions.q: How has digital technology changed post-production?
flashcard_questions.a: It has lowered costs and made post-production accessible on standard laptops, reducing barriers for independent producers.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the gig economy in media?
flashcard_questions.a: A working model where individuals take short-term freelance contracts, bearing the financial risk of fluctuating demand.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does budget level in pre-production matter for the finished product?
flashcard_questions.a: Budget determines what technology, cast, locations and crew are available, shaping the product's visual and audio style.

glossary_terms.definition: The planning phase before filming or recording begins, including scripting, casting, budgeting and scheduling.
A detailed timeline that sets out when each stage of production will happen and who is responsible for it.
A senior creative and managerial figure who oversees a television series across all episodes, responsible for both the writing and the day-to-day production.
The editing, mixing, grading and other technical processes applied to raw footage or recordings after the main production phase.
Hiring outside companies or individuals to carry out work rather than doing it in-house.
Commissioning and producing content primarily intended for streaming rather than traditional broadcast or cinema release, often with all episodes released simultaneously.

hero_image_caption: A production crew working on set, illustrating the collaborative process behind media products.
